clinicalPearls: Kernicterus refers to the neurological injury caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, classically in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
It is a preventable complication of severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and represents the chronic, permanent form of bilirubin neurotoxicity.

Acute bilirubin encephalopathy evolves through phases: early lethargy, hypotonia, and poor feeding, followed by hypertonia with backward arching (retrocollis and opisthotonus), high-pitched cry, and fever, and later apnoea, seizures, and coma.
The classic chronic tetrad includes choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (or auditory neuropathy), impaired upward gaze, and dental enamel dysplasia.
Only unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin that is not bound to albumin can cross the blood-brain barrier, so free bilirubin and factors lowering albumin binding increase risk.
Prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, and certain drugs that displace bilirubin heighten vulnerability at any given bilirubin level.
Prevention rests on identifying and monitoring at-risk newborns, timely phototherapy, and exchange transfusion when bilirubin approaches neurotoxic thresholds.
Once established, chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is largely irreversible, underscoring the importance of early recognition and treatment of hyperbilirubinaemia.
Structured predischarge risk assessment and follow-up of jaundiced newborns reduce the incidence of this now-rare but devastating condition.
reference.pathophysiology: Unconjugated bilirubin is normally tightly bound to albumin and does not enter the brain. When the bilirubin load overwhelms albumin binding capacity, or binding is reduced by acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, prematurity, or competing substances, free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is neurotoxic, being preferentially deposited in and damaging the basal ganglia (notably the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei), the brainstem auditory and oculomotor nuclei, hippocampus, and cerebellum. Bilirubin impairs mitochondrial function and neuronal signalling, causing acute dysfunction and, if sustained, permanent neuronal loss and gliosis with the characteristic clinical sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Inborn errors of metabolism causing encephalopathy
Other causes of neonatal hypertonia or abnormal movements
additionalInvestigations: Serial total and unconjugated bilirubin, interpreted against age-in-hours nomograms
Albumin level and bilirubin-to-albumin ratio to gauge binding reserve
Haemolysis workup (blood group, direct antiglobulin test, blood film, reticulocytes)
Auditory brainstem response testing for auditory neuropathy
MRI showing characteristic basal ganglia signal changes in established disease
Evaluation for contributing factors such as sepsis, acidosis, and prematurity
redFlags: Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy or hypertonia, retrocollis/opisthotonus, high-pitched cry, poor feeding
Bilirubin approaching or exceeding exchange transfusion thresholds for the infant's age and risk
Apnoea, seizures, or coma in a severely jaundiced newborn
Rapidly rising bilirubin, especially with haemolysis, sepsis, or acidosis
Jaundice in a preterm or unwell infant where binding reserve is reduced
reference.prognosis: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy may be partly reversible if bilirubin is lowered promptly, but progression to chronic kernicterus produces permanent, often severe disability including movement disorder, hearing loss, and gaze abnormalities. Because the condition is largely preventable, prognosis hinges on timely detection and treatment of severe hyperbilirubinaemia.
pitfalls: Interpreting bilirubin values without reference to the infant's age in hours and risk factors
Underestimating neurotoxic risk in preterm, acidotic, hypoalbuminaemic, or septic infants at lower bilirubin levels
Delaying phototherapy or exchange transfusion while bilirubin rises
Missing early, subtle neurological signs of acute encephalopathy
Discharging a jaundiced newborn without adequate follow-up and risk assessment
management: Intensive phototherapy to lower unconjugated bilirubin as the primary intervention in acute bilirubin encephalopathy
Exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly rising hyperbilirubinaemia or signs of acute encephalopathy
Intravenous immunoglobulin for isoimmune haemolytic disease to reduce ongoing haemolysis
Correction of aggravating factors such as sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia and dehydration that increase free bilirubin and neurotoxicity
Treatment of the underlying cause of haemolysis with adequate hydration and feeding support
Long-term management of choreoathetoid cerebral palsy with medications and rehabilitation therapies, and cochlear implantation or hearing aids for auditory neuropathy
Multidisciplinary developmental, audiological and visual follow-up, with prevention through timely bilirubin screening against age-in-hours nomograms
